entities.name: California Institute of Technology
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The California Institute of Technology (Caltech), founded in 1891 in Pasadena by Amos Throop as a vocational school and transformed into a world-class research university by physicist Robert Millikan in 1921, has the highest Nobel Prize per-capita rate of any university in the world — 72 Nobel laureates from an institution with only 2,300 students. Caltech operates NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and has managed the majority of America's robotic space exploration program, including the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance.

Caltech's transformation began when Robert Millikan (Nobel 1923 for measuring electron charge) came from Chicago in 1921 and recruited the world's best physicists. Richard Feynman's Caltech lectures (1961-1963) became the greatest physics textbooks ever written (The Feynman Lectures on Physics). Linus Pauling developed quantum chemistry and crystal structure analysis at Caltech, winning two Nobel Prizes (Chemistry 1954, Peace 1962 — the only person to win two unshared Nobels).

JPL, managed by Caltech under NASA contract since 1958, has operated every American robotic solar system mission — Voyager 1 and 2 (now beyond the solar system), Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, and the Ingenuity helicopter (first powered flight on another planet). Caltech's LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory), developed with MIT, detected gravitational waves for the first time in 2015 — confirming Einstein's 100-year-old prediction and creating an entirely new astronomical instrument.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Caltech's JPL management of NASA's robotic solar system exploration — from Voyager beyond the solar system to Perseverance on Mars — combined with LIGO's gravitational wave detection makes it the university with the greatest contribution to expanding humanity's physical knowledge of the cosmos.
